newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada seen using dollar against inflation.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada seen using dollar against inflation.

text.p: Canada's central bank is expected to use the strengthening Canadian dollar to keep the country's economy from overheating, while holding interest rates at their lowest levels in 40 years to spur consumers.

"The bottom line here is the Bank (of Canada) will tolerate tightening in monetary conditions coming from the currency without doing anything (on interest rates)," said Anita Lauria, economist at Salomon Brothers in New York.
In the past two years, the Bank of Canada has cut interest rates to stimulate economic growth each time the country's currency has risen.

Despite booming exports fueled by the relatively cheap dollar, Canada's economy limped along last year, with consumers reluctant to spend because of high unemployment, deep government cutbacks and heavy debt.
Consumer spending accounts for about 60 percent of Canada's gross domestic product.

With stronger Canadian growth expected this year, economists predicted the Bank of Canada would let the currency rise to thwart any possible resurgence of inflation, while keeping rates low to revive consumer spending.

Although most economists agreed Canada's consumer price index would stay within the Bank of Canada's one to three percent target range this year, they saw more of an inflation risk as Canada's productivity level edged closer toward capacity.
"In the Canadian economy, we are only recently seeing signs that low interest rates are feeding through (into economic growth)," noted Craig Wright, deputy chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada.

"That suggests the Bank of Canada is starting to get some payback for the low interest rate environment and that they would not want to be too quick out of the blocks to rein in growth from the interest rate front."
Economists said the central bank would signal the policy shift simply by not cutting rates again, despite a recent rally that has sent the Canadian dollar near its highest levels in more than a year.
"If the Bank (of Canada) doesn't cut rates again over the next few days, the mother of all signals has been sent," said Andrew Spence, senior economist for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Canada Ltd.

Since Jan. 2 the Canadian dollar has risen more than two U.S. cents to its current level of about 74.75 U.S. cents, less than half a cent above the level at which the central bank last reduced interest rates on Nov. 8.
At that time the Bank of Canada cited the rise of the Canadian dollar to "a new higher trading range" as its reason for cutting interest rates.

That was the latest in a series of interest rate cuts since May 1995 that slashed Canadian rates by five percentage points. Canadian banks have responded by reducing their commercial lending rates to their lowest levels in 41 years.

Last week, the central bank defended its current interest rate targets by intervening in the currency in the money markets as the dollar surged and analysts forecast the Canadian currency could climb to 80 U.S. cents by year's end.
Economists attributed the stronger Canadian dollar to expectations that Canada would vie with France for the strongest growth this year among G7 industrial countries.
Nesbitt Burns economist Doug Porter forecast that Canada's gross domestic product would grow by 3.3 percent in 1997 versus an estimated 1.4 percent gain in 1996.
"We're pretty bullish on the economy," Porter said.
